newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia to launch benchmark bonds in Sept.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia to launch benchmark bonds in Sept.

text.p: Malaysia will launch its first benchmark bond in September aimed at providing a price peg for corporate debt issues, government and industry sources said on Tuesday.
The long-awaited bonds will be launched by Khazanah Nasional Bhd, the investment arm for the government, they said.
"The issues have almost been finalised and it is certain that we will launch in September," a senior government official told Reuters.
Khazanah has planned to launch a three-year Islamic bond of 500 million to one billion ringgit, the sources said.
The three-year bond will be followed by a series of varying maturities of five, seven and 10 years.
The benchmark bond issue was announced in the government's annual budget for 1997 in October last year.
Targetted for launch in the first quarter of this year, the launch of the bonds has been delayed due to protracted debate over their structuring, the sources said.
"Some issues still need to be cleared, but the issue and its structure itself has been finalised," an industry source said.
He said it has been decided that for lower than three-years tenure, the benchmark yield curve will use one-year interbank or swap rates.
But, the question from the banks was how they would calculate their cost of funds for the purposes of this bond issue, since they did not qualify for liquid asset status.
Banks in Malaysia have to maintain a certain amount of their total liabilities in government paper and place some funds as interest-free cash with the central bank.
It was also not clear how much gap would be kept between lower yield treasury issues and the benchmark bonds, sources said.
Prospective buyers were also seeking permission from authorities for the bonds to qualify for investment by provident or pension funds.

The sources said the bonds would be issued in the same manner as treasury bill issues. A tender would be issued and all prospective buyers would have to bid through the central bank-appointed principal dealers.

The government has been trying various methods to activate the country's moribund debt market. While the number of issues has grown sharply over the past five years, a secondary market has been virtually absent.

In an article in its monthly newsletter for June, the Rating Agency Malaysia (RAM) said, "the proposed Khazanah benchmark issues will take the form of zero-coupon Islamic bonds based on the Al-Murabahah principles."
Under Islam's Sharia principles, business should be done on the basis of sale and purchase of assets. Giving loans by charging interest is considered usury.
Al-Murabahah refers to sale and purchase of goods at a price with built in profit.
RAM said the aim of the issues was to provide risk-free debt papers over a range of maturities.

"Through active market-making and trading of these bonds, a yield curve can then be constructed to serve as a bellwether for interest rate expectations and as a benchmark for the pricing of other bond issues," it said in the article.
